explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The people grumble against Moses, Israel's leader, and ask, “What are we to drink?” (Exodus 15:24). Three days of walking with no water will do that to a crowd. I think I'd be asking somebody that question too, and I'd be loud about it.

The text never says anyone picks up a shovel. What it says is that the people grumble against Moses, Israel's leader, and ask, “What are we to drink?” (Exodus 15:24). The only thing that gets dug up at Marah is a complaint.

The text doesn't say the people pray or that anyone asks for rain. They grumble against Moses, Israel's leader, and ask, “What are we to drink?” (Exodus 15:24). The one who cries out to the LORD in this scene is Moses, and that comes next.

explanations.answer: He cries out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't answer the grumbling with a speech. He cries out to the LORD, and the LORD shows him a log (Exodus 15:25). I love that order, because he goes to the right place first. Take it from a stamper who spent years in a drawer: when you're stuck, start there.

explanations.answer: He sends men to dig a well
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any digging. It says Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log (Exodus 15:25). The help at Marah comes from the LORD's answer, not from a work crew.

explanations.answer: He leads them back toward the sea
explanations.explanation: Nobody turns around in this scene. Moses cries out to the LORD, and the LORD shows him a log (Exodus 15:25). After that, the people go on to Elim (Exodus 15:27), so the camp keeps moving forward.
Sweet is the word. When Moses cast the log into the waters, “they were sweetened” (Exodus 15:25). Bitter water went in one end and drinkable water came out the other. The LORD made it happen.

The text doesn't say anything about how the water looked. It says that when Moses cast the log in, the waters “were sweetened” (Exodus 15:25). The problem was the bitter taste, and that's what changed.
The text never mentions the temperature. It says the waters “were sweetened” when Moses cast the log in (Exodus 15:25). The change was in the taste, so sweet is the answer.

Diseases is the word. The LORD says, “then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians” (Exodus 15:26). The promise comes with an if, because He's asking them to listen carefully, do what is right in His eyes, and keep His commands. It's a promise worth holding onto.

Droughts aren't mentioned here, even though these folks just walked three days without water. The LORD says, “then I will not bring on you any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians” (Exodus 15:26). The word is diseases.
No earthquakes show up in this passage. The LORD says He won't bring on them “any of the diseases I inflicted on the Egyptians” (Exodus 15:26). The word He uses is diseases.
True. The LORD says, “For I am the LORD who heals you” (Exodus 15:26). He says it right there at the water He just sweetened. I'd say that's a good place to hear it.
This one is actually true. At Marah the LORD says, “For I am the LORD who heals you” (Exodus 15:26). He says it after telling them to listen carefully to His voice and keep His commands.

explanations.answer: Twelve springs and seventy palm trees
explanations.explanation: That's Elim. The text says there were “twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees,” and the people camped there by the waters (Exodus 15:27). Water and shade, right after all that dry walking. I think that camp felt like a vacation.

explanations.answer: Twelve stones from the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: No stones are mentioned at Elim. The text says there were “twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees,” and they camped there by the waters (Exodus 15:27). The number twelve is there, but it belongs to the springs.

explanations.answer: A well dug by the princes
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any well at Elim. It says there were “twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees,” and the people camped there by the waters (Exodus 15:27). The water at Elim was already flowing.

explanations.answer: Pots of meat and plenty of bread
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread” (Exodus 16:3). Notice what they remember: the meals. I think hunger has a way of making the past look like a buffet.
The people don't mention homes or clothes. They say, “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread” (Exodus 16:3). Their complaint is about what's on the table.
The Nile doesn't come up in their complaint. They say, “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread” (Exodus 16:3). They're remembering meat and bread.

This one is false. The LORD says, “Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day” (Exodus 16:4). It's a day at a time, not a week at a time. That's a lot like how I'd bake a single batch for one day, then do it again tomorrow.
False is right. The LORD says, “Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day” (Exodus 16:4). Each day has its own gathering, so nobody is told to stock up for the week.

explanations.answer: To test whether they will follow His instructions
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. He says, “In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions” (Exodus 16:4). The daily gathering is how that test works. The text states the reason itself, so we don't have to guess.

explanations.answer: To keep the camp from getting too crowded
explanations.explanation: Crowding never comes up. The LORD says, “In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions” (Exodus 16:4). The reason given is the test.

explanations.answer: To teach them how to trade with each other
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says anything about trading. The LORD says, “In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions” (Exodus 16:4). That's the reason He gives for the daily gathering.

True. The LORD says, “Then on the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on the other days” (Exodus 16:5). So the sixth day has a double portion built in. Hold onto that detail, because it matters later.
This one is true. The LORD says that on the sixth day, what they bring in “will be twice as much as they gather on the other days” (Exodus 16:5). The sixth day is the day with the double portion.

The LORD. Moses says, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD” (Exodus 16:8). He and Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), are just the ones standing in front of the crowd. He also asks, “Who are we?”, which sounds like a man who knows he's only the messenger.
The elders aren't named in this part. Moses says, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD” (Exodus 16:8). The word he uses is the LORD.

The Egyptians aren't who Moses points to here. He says, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD” (Exodus 16:8). The people are grumbling right there in the desert, and Moses says it's against the LORD.

A cloud. As Aaron is speaking, the people look toward the desert, “and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared” (Exodus 16:10). Right in the middle of the speech, they all turn and look. I'd have stopped talking too.

The burning bush was something Moses saw earlier, when the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from within a bush (Exodus 3:2). This time, “in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared” (Exodus 16:10). The whole congregation is looking toward the desert when it happens.
The text doesn't mention lightning. It says the congregation looked toward the desert, “and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared” (Exodus 16:10). The glory of the LORD appears in a cloud.
Quail. “That evening quail came and covered the camp” (Exodus 16:13). Moses had said the LORD would give them meat that evening (Exodus 16:8), and here it is right on time. Covered the camp, friend.
Locusts aren't in this scene. The text says, “That evening quail came and covered the camp” (Exodus 16:13). Quail is the answer.
No ravens here. The text says, “That evening quail came and covered the camp” (Exodus 16:13). Quail is the answer.

That's the question. The Israelites ask one another, “What is it?” because “they did not know what it was” (Exodus 16:15). Then Moses tells them it's the bread the LORD has given them to eat. They had no idea what they were looking at, and I think that's a fair reaction.
That's not what they ask. They say, “What is it?” because “they did not know what it was” (Exodus 16:15). Moses then answers them.

The text doesn't say they ask that. They ask one another, “What is it?” because “they did not know what it was” (Exodus 16:15). Moses is the one who tells them it's the bread the LORD has given them to eat.

True. When they measured it by the omer, “he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (Exodus 16:18). Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat. Nobody went hungry, and I think that's pretty wonderful.
This one is true. The text says, “he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (Exodus 16:18). Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat.

This one is false. Moses said no one may keep any of it until morning, but “they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning” (Exodus 16:20). So some listened and some didn't. The text says it was some people, not everyone.
False is right. The text says, “they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning” (Exodus 16:20). That's how the maggots enter the story.

explanations.answer: It gets maggots and starts to smell
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The leftover manna “became infested with maggots and began to smell” (Exodus 16:20). That's one way to find out the bread doesn't keep overnight. I've forgotten a batch on the counter, but never one like that.

explanations.answer: It turns as hard as a rock
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say it hardens. It says the leftover manna “became infested with maggots and began to smell” (Exodus 16:20). Maggots and smell are the answer.

explanations.answer: It blows away in the wind
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say the wind takes it. It says the leftover manna “became infested with maggots and began to smell” (Exodus 16:20). It stayed right there with the people who kept it.

True. “Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away” (Exodus 16:21). So the gathering happens in the morning, before the heat. I think that's one early shift.
This one is true. The text says, “Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away” (Exodus 16:21). So the bread melts once the sun is hot.

That's what Moses says. “Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (Exodus 16:23). The double portion on the sixth day sets it up. The people get a day to rest, and the bread is already covered.
Moses doesn't say anything about moving camp. He says, “Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (Exodus 16:23). It's a day to stay put and rest.

explanations.answer: A day to gather even more
explanations.explanation: No more gathering is called for. Moses says, “Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD” (Exodus 16:23). The gathering has already been done on the sixth day, with its double portion.

True. “So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots” (Exodus 16:24). Same overnight wait, but a totally different result. It happens this time because Moses told them to do it.

This one is true. The text says, “So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots” (Exodus 16:24). Compare that to the leftovers from before, which smelled and had maggots.

That's what Moses says. “For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there” (Exodus 16:26). So there's no reason to go looking. I think he's telling them the field will be empty.

explanations.answer: Only half of it will fall
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't mention half. He says, “For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there” (Exodus 16:26). On the seventh day it won't be there at all.

Moses doesn't tell them to get up early on the seventh day. He says, “For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there” (Exodus 16:26). There's nothing to gather on that day.

Stay. The LORD says, “On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place” (Exodus 16:29). He says this right after telling them He has given them the Sabbath. Stay put, friend.

The LORD isn't telling them to gather on the seventh day. He says, “On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place” (Exodus 16:29). Gathering is for the other six days.
Building isn't mentioned. The LORD says, “On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place” (Exodus 16:29). The word is stay.

explanations.answer: So future generations can see it
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Moses gives. The LORD commanded, “Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 16:32). The manna is kept so those who come later can see it. That's a good thing to put in a jar.

explanations.answer: So they have food if it runs out
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason given. The command is to keep an omer of manna “for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness” (Exodus 16:32). The point is for later generations to see it.

explanations.answer: So Aaron can offer it on the altar
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says to keep an omer of manna “for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness” (Exodus 16:32). Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), puts the jar in front of the Testimony to be preserved (Exodus 16:34).

Years. “The Israelites ate manna forty years” (Exodus 16:35), until they reached the border of Canaan. Forty years of the same morning gift. I can barely bake one more batch on a Monday, and they got this every day.
Days is far too short. The text says, “The Israelites ate manna forty years” (Exodus 16:35). They ate it until they reached the border of Canaan.
Weeks is much too short. The text says, “The Israelites ate manna forty years” (Exodus 16:35). They kept eating it until they reached the border of Canaan.
